strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem: activation quantization of large vision encoders, where outliers severely degrade low-bit performance. The proposed RegCache is a training-free, plug-in method that can be combined with existing PTQ algorithms.

It provides useful empirical characterizations of outliers in vision encoders: unlike LLMs, outliers emerge in middle layers, are associated with semantically uninformative background patches, and are highly similar across images, motivating the use of cached register tokens.

The method is simple and well motivated: curate register candidates from reference images, cache/insert their KV entries into middle-to-final layers, and delete emerging outlier tokens at the quantization-sensitive layer. The ablation and appendix analyses clarify the roles of caching and deletion.

Experiments are extensive across five vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2), several PTQ baselines (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q), multiple bit-widths, classification and retrieval tasks, and additional settings such as weight-only quantization and Hadamard rotation. Many low-bit results show large gains.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and includes limitations, computational overhead analysis, and transfer experiments, making the empirical case reasonably transparent.
weaknesses: The method requires per-model and per-base-quantization hyperparameter tuning: identifying the quantization-sensitive layer, selecting top-k register candidates, choosing the number of inserted copies, and deciding how many tokens to delete. This tuning relies on labeled reference data and a validation search (about 1 hour on an RTX 4090), so the 'training-free' claim does not mean tuning-free or data-free.

The empirical gains are not as consistent as claimed. For example, DINOv2-B/14 at W8A8 shows a negative average gap (-0.62), and some FIMA-Q/SigLIP2 and weight-only settings also degrade slightly. The paper states RegCache 'consistently improves' accuracy, which overstates the evidence.

Novelty is incremental: the core idea of prefixing attention-sink/register tokens to mitigate outliers is adapted from LLM quantization work such as PrefixQuant, and the vision-specific modifications (middle-layer prefixing and token deletion) are mostly empirical. The paper's contribution is primarily a well-executed adaptation rather than a fundamentally new algorithm.

The theoretical explanation in the appendix (Lemma 1) is a stylized argument that high cosine similarity follows from large-magnitude entries in aligned channels; it does not fully explain why such outliers emerge in middle layers or why the proposed intervention should generalize across architectures.

The ablation discussion is partially inconsistent with the table: for SigLIP2, token deletion alone improves accuracy dramatically (26.04 to 69.06), yet the text says applying only one step gives worse results than the naive case. This weakens confidence in the interpretation of the two components.

Token deletion is a heuristic that removes the top-k largest-norm tokens at the sensitive layer; although visualizations suggest these are background patches, there is limited analysis of failure cases or of how often semantically relevant tokens might be deleted.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the paper does not mention code release, and the exact reference/calibration splits and per-model hyperparameters are not fully specified, making independent reproduction harder.

strengths: The paper reports a genuinely novel and well-supported empirical observation: activation outliers in vision encoders emerge in the *middle* layers (Fig. 2), in contrast to LLMs where they appear in early layers. This is a useful scientific finding that motivates the proposed method and is likely to inform future quantization and interpretability work.

The finding that outlier tokens are highly similar across different images (mean cosine similarity 0.89 vs. 0.26 for normal tokens, Table 1), supporting the 'universal register' hypothesis, is a compelling insight. The paper backs it with a simple theoretical argument (Lemma 1) linking high cosine similarity to aligned large-magnitude channels, and with an analysis of foreground-only images (Fig. 3).

RegCache is training-free and plug-in: it consistently improves accuracy when combined with multiple existing PTQ methods (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q) across five vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2), several bit-widths (4/6/8-bit), and two tasks (zero-shot classification and image–text retrieval). The breadth of the empirical study is a real strength.

The paper is thorough: it includes ablations (caching vs. deleting, Table 6), a reduction in maximum token norm (Table 5), weight-only quantization (Table 11), computational efficiency (Table 12), comparison with a test-time register approach (Table 14), and generalization to other datasets (Table 4), giving good evidence that the method is broadly applicable.
Practicality is demonstrated: the added FLOPs are <0.2% and latency overhead is small, and the method operates on top of existing pipelines without retraining.

The manuscript is clearly written, well organized, and honestly discusses limitations and future directions, including the differing outlier behavior of DINOv2 and the tokenization perspective on why vision encoders differ from LLMs (Sec. J).
weaknesses: The 'training-free' framing is somewhat overstated. The method requires a pool of 50,000 reference images and a *labeled* reference task (ImageNet-1k) to (i) identify the quantization-sensitive layer, (ii) tune the number of prefix copies τ, and (iii) tune the number of tokens to delete. This is closer to calibration/validation-based tuning than a truly training-free or calibration-free procedure, and the reliance on labeled reference data may limit applicability in settings where such labels are unavailable.

Several hyperparameters (the prefix-insertion layer, the number of prefix tokens τ, and the number of deleted tokens k̃) are selected heuristically per encoder and per base quantizer. The paper acknowledges this, but it weakens the claim of a 'versatile and go-to' method and raises questions about robustness and the effort required to apply RegCache to a new model.

The gains are not uniform: on DINOv2 the improvements at W8A8 are negligible or slightly negative (Best Δ −0.05, Average Δ −0.62 in Table 2), and this is not deeply explained beyond a brief note about self-supervised training. This inconsistency deserves more analysis, especially since DINOv2 is one of the five evaluated encoders.

The mechanism by which prefixing register tokens suppresses outliers is demonstrated empirically (Table 5 shows reduced max token norm) but not fully explained. The link to attention sinks is plausible but somewhat heuristic, and the paper does not rigorously establish why inserted prefixes absorb the outlier behavior of other tokens.

The most directly related competitor—the test-time register approach of Jiang et al. [14]—is compared only in the appendix (Table 14). Given that it is the closest prior work on register tokens for outlier mitigation, a more prominent and thorough comparison (including at multiple bit-widths and tasks) would strengthen the paper.

Some design choices are reasonable but under-ablated: e.g., averaging the KV caches over the top-k register candidates (Sec. 4.2) and restricting prefix insertion to middle-to-final layers. The sensitivity to these choices is only partially explored (Fig. 8, Sec. L).

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: activation quantization of large vision encoders for edge/real-time deployment, where outliers remain a key obstacle even at 8-bit.

Provides genuinely interesting empirical observations: (i) unlike LLMs, outliers in vision encoders emerge gradually in middle-to-final blocks, and (ii) outlier tokens are highly similar across images (cosine ~0.89 vs 0.26 for normal tokens), motivating the use of a pre-computed universal register.
The proposed RegCache is training-free and designed as a plug-in on top of existing PTQ methods, which is a desirable property for practical adoption.

Experiments are broad and thorough: five vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2), three base quantization families (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant) plus FIMA-Q and AWQ, 4/6/8-bit settings, classification (ImageNet-1k and four transfer datasets) and retrieval (MS-COCO), with ablations, efficiency analysis, and comparison to test-time registers.

Improvements are large in the most challenging low-bit regimes (e.g., CLIP-B/16 W4A4 RepQ-ViT 1.83 -> 21.50), and the paper provides useful analyses (max-token-norm reduction, register visualization, prefix-insertion-layer sensitivity, tokenization-perspective discussion).
The paper is generally clearly written and well organized, and reproducibility details (reference pool, k, tau, search cost) are largely provided.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The central idea -- prefixing attention-sink/register tokens to absorb activation outliers -- is directly adapted from LLM work (Son et al. [31]) combined with registers (Darcet et al. [7]). The claimed new elements (middle-layer insertion and token deletion) are incremental refinements rather than a fundamentally new contribution, and the paper itself frames the method as a vision-domain transfer of the LLM recipe.

The ablation in Table 6 does not convincingly support the claimed synergy. Token deletion alone catastrophically degrades SigLIP-B/16 (69.71 -> 42.41) while greatly helping SigLIP2-B/16; and for SigLIP prefix caching plus deletion (74.38) is essentially identical to prefix caching alone (74.37). The components therefore behave inconsistently across models, and the 'complementary/synergistic' claim is overstated relative to the evidence.

The 'training-free' framing is somewhat misleading. RegCache requires a pool of 50k reference images, per-model identification of quantization-sensitive layers, and validation-based tuning of tau*, k, and the deletion count k-tilde on a reference task (reported as ~1 hour of search). This is a data- and compute-dependent procedure that undermines the simple plug-and-play narrative and complicates fair comparison to baselines that do not use such search.

Results are not uniformly positive. DINOv2-B/14 slightly regresses under W8A8 (Best Delta -0.05, Average Delta -0.62), and several SigLIP/SigLIP2 settings show only marginal or negative gains (e.g., Table 8, SigLIP2 -0.09/-0.10). The paper does not adequately analyze when/why the method fails to help.

The theoretical support (Lemma 1 in Appendix B) is a stylized asymptotic argument about high-norm aligned coordinates; it offers limited insight into why inserting pre-computed registers actually reduces outliers in a quantized network, so the core mechanism remains largely justified by analogy to LLMs rather than analysis.

The most closely related method (test-time registers of Jiang et al. [14]) is only compared in a single small table (Table 14) with a brief discussion; given how conceptually close this baseline is, a more thorough head-to-head comparison would be expected.

The proposed pipeline introduces multiple heuristics (reference pool size, k, tau range, k-tilde, which layers to prefix) and the sensitivity of these choices is only partially explored, raising concerns about robustness across new architectures.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: activation quantization of large vision encoders for efficient deployment, especially in low-bit regimes where outliers severely degrade PTQ.

Provides a useful empirical analysis of outliers/sink tokens in vision encoders versus LLMs, showing they emerge in middle layers, are highly similar across images, and are linked to continuous tokenization rather than discrete vocabularies.
Proposes RegCache, a simple training-free plugin combining reference-based register prefix caching with token deletion; it is compatible with multiple PTQ baselines and model architectures.

Experimental evidence is broad: five vision encoders, 4/6/8-bit settings, ImageNet classification, MS-COCO retrieval, additional classification datasets, VLM image/video benchmarks, latency measurements, and many appendix ablations/analyses.
Demonstrates consistent gains over strong PTQ baselines, with particularly large improvements in low-bit settings and only modest latency overhead.

Includes informative visualizations and analyses (layerwise sensitivity, max token norms, foreground/background experiments, cosine similarity, prefix visualization) that make the method more interpretable.
Discusses limitations and provides many implementation details, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' claim is qualified: the main method uses the ImageNet-1k training split as a reference set to identify sensitive layers, curate candidate registers, and tune the number of inserted prefix tokens and deleted tokens, so it still requires labeled reference data and hyperparameter search.

Component attribution is not fully convincing. Table 8 shows token deletion alone can be catastrophic for SigLIP but nearly sufficient for SigLIP2, while prefix caching alone can be harmful for SigLIP2; the claimed synergy is inconsistent, and component ablations are missing for CLIP/OpenCLIP/DINOv2.

The method changes the token sequence by deleting top-norm tokens. For models with patch-wise pooling (SigLIP/SigLIP2), it is not fully explained how inserted/deleted tokens affect the final representation or whether the comparisons remain strictly fair; robustness to deleting informative tokens is not thoroughly analyzed.

Some reported gains are extremely large and uneven (e.g., DINOv2 W4A4 RepQ-ViT 4.52→82.97; SigLIP W6A6 0.77→72.38), which merits more scrutiny and isolation of whether gains come from quantization-range reduction, token deletion, or evaluation artifacts.

Hyperparameters (number of prefix tokens, deletion count, insertion layer, number of preceding blocks) are model- and quantizer-specific and are tuned with reference-task accuracy, limiting plug-and-play applicability and adding tuning overhead that is not fully quantified.

The central claim that vision encoders 'need' prefixing registers is stronger than the evidence: for at least one model, token deletion alone captures most of the gain, so the necessity of prefixing is not conclusively established.
Comparison with concurrent test-time register work is limited to a small W8A8 setting, and no code release is mentioned, which may hinder reproducibility and adoption.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated empirical insight: the paper shows that activation outliers in vision encoders differ from LLMs—emerging in middle layers, often corresponding to background patches, and highly similar across images—which enables a universal register-based mitigation strategy.

Simple, training-free, and practical plug-in method: RegCache curates register candidates from reference images, caches their KV representations, prefixes them into the vision encoder, and deletes remaining outlier tokens, requiring no model training and only marginal inference overhead.

Extensive and convincing empirical validation: experiments span five standalone vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2), multiple bit widths (8/6/4-bit), classification and retrieval tasks, and VLM settings (Qwen3-VL, LLaVA), with consistent gains especially in low-bit regimes.

Thorough analysis and ablation: layerwise quantization sensitivity, outlier reduction, prefix visualization, generalization to other datasets, latency measurement, label-free variant, test-time register comparison, weight-only quantization, Hadamard rotation, and SmoothQuant combinations strengthen the paper.
Clear presentation and strong practical relevance: the method is easy to integrate into existing PTQ pipelines, and the paper acknowledges limitations and discusses future directions.
weaknesses: The method requires tuning several hyperparameters and selecting reference images from ImageNet-1k, which may introduce some dependence on the reference domain; the label-free reconstruction-loss variant is weaker than the ImageNet-tuned version.

Some ablation results indicate that individual components can be unstable: prefix caching alone can hurt SigLIP2, and token deletion alone can severely hurt SigLIP, suggesting the synergy is not fully explained and the method may be somewhat brittle across models.
Main results lack variance or error bars, and no code/artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility and makes it harder to assess statistical significance.

The quantization-sensitive layer is identified using W8A8 sensitivity; it is not fully clear that this choice transfers optimally to 4-bit quantization settings, and DINOv2 shows a negligible negative gain at W8A8.
The paper includes only limited discussion of broader societal impact, though this is not a central weakness for this technical contribution.

strengths: Targets a timely and under-explored problem: activation quantization for vision encoders, which lags behind the LLM PTQ literature despite being compute-bound in deployment and VLM pipelines.

Provides a clear and well-supported empirical characterization: outliers in vision encoders emerge in middle MLP (FC2) layers (Fig. 3, Fig. 6), in contrast to the early-layer emergence in LLMs, with a plausible tokenization-based explanation (Sec. M).

Reports an interesting and useful finding that middle-layer outlier tokens are highly similar across images (Table 1, mean cosine 0.89 vs. 0.26 for normal tokens), motivating the 'universal register' hypothesis.
The method is training-free and plug-in, and is shown to compose with a diverse set of PTQ baselines (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, ERQ), weight-only quantization, and Hadamard rotation.
Experiments are broad: five vision encoders, image classification, retrieval, VLM (Qwen3-VL, LLaVA), and video benchmarks, with ablations, latency measurements, and an extensive appendix.
Latency overhead is small (≤1.54%) and the analysis of prefix-insertion layer sensitivity (Fig. 8) and segmentation impact (Table 12) is informative.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially an adaptation of LLM prefix/sink-token mitigation (PrefixQuant, Xiao et al.) combined with register tokens (Darcet et al.) plus a token-deletion heuristic. The vision-specific twist (middle-layer insertion and deletion) is modest, and the key observations overlap substantially with cited concurrent work (Jiang et al. 2025; Sun et al.).

Hyperparameters (number of prefix copies τ*, number of deleted tokens k̄, prefix-insertion layer, quantization-sensitive layer) are selected per encoder and per base quantization algorithm by maximizing ImageNet-1k training-split accuracy — the same domain as the primary evaluation. This risks tuning-on-evaluation-domain, complicates fair comparison with baselines, and is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation, weakening practical utility and reproducibility.

The theoretical justification (Lemma 1) is essentially trivial: high cosine similarity of 'spiked' vectors follows immediately from a dominant shared coordinate. It adds little explanatory power and does not substantiate the stronger universality claim.

The 'universal register' claim is overstated. Generalization is only validated on ImageNet-1k-derived classification datasets (Table 5), and DINOv2 shows negligible or even slightly negative gains, indicating the method is not universally applicable across vision encoders.

The direct comparison to the most relevant concurrent approach (Jiang et al. test-time register) is relegated to Appendix B under a single W8A8 setting, which is not a comprehensive or clearly fair comparison given the method's core claim of being preferable to register-based suppression.

Some reported gains are implausibly large (e.g., +57 points for DINOv2, +50 points for SigLIP2 on some datasets), and the paper does not fully disentangle the contribution of prefix caching, token deletion, and per-model hyperparameter tuning; the ablation (Table 8) shows that using either component alone can be worse than the naive baseline, which raises questions about the robustness of the mechanism.

Reliance on a large fixed reference pool (50,000 ImageNet-1k images) for curation and on the ImageNet-1k training split for hyperparameter search is not ablated for sensitivity, limiting confidence in deployment on restricted or shifted data despite the reconstruction-loss variant in Appendix K.
